entry.title: Inside the reactor: Exploring Molten Salt Technology

media:group.media:title: Inside the reactor: Exploring Molten Salt Technology
media:group.media:description:
Molten salt reactors (MSRs) are a promising technology currently being explored as a potential option for the future of nuclear energy. In MSRs, the fuel is dissolved in the molten salt, which is then circulated to transfer the heat. But how does a reactor work when the fuel is liquid? What happens inside the reactor core? This animation explains the basic principle of a molten salt reactor – from the role of the fuel salt and nuclear fission to the structure and operation of the reactor core. Using the “Onion Core” concept developed by Copenhagen Atomics as an example, the video shows how the various components interact. It provides insight into the potential benefits of this technology and the challenges that still need to be overcome.
Chapters: 00:00 Introduction with examples of human energy consumption 00:36 Introduction to the molten salt reactor as a new development in nuclear research 00:47 Salt as a fuel and carrier material 01:23 Nuclear fission as the central physical reaction 02:10 The onion-core reactor design and its components 02:41 Operations and processes in the reactor core 03:05 Safety characteristics of the reactor 03:55 Advantages, such as fuel flexibility 04:06 Disadvantages and challenges, such as radioactive waste, material stability, and complex licensing procedures 04:32 Outro

entry.title: How to produce sustainable aviation fuel?

media:group.media:title: How to produce sustainable aviation fuel?
media:group.media:description:
Energy researcher Marco Ranocchiari guides us through the new «aerobrew» demonstration plant at the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI. Here, in collaboration with the company Metafuels, a process is being tested that produces sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from methanol.
The demonstration plant serves to test the technology under real-world conditions and to collect data for a planned commercial plant. In the long term, the required methanol will be produced from carbon dioxide using sustainable sources and green hydrogen.

entry.title: Electric cars put to the scientific test | Beat fragt

media:group.media:title: Electric cars put to the scientific test | Beat fragt
media:group.media:description:
Some people believe that electric cars are the solution to climate change. Others think they’re too expensive, impractical or just a fad. We’re going to take a closer look at the most common questions surrounding electric cars.
How much carbon dioxide does an electric car really save? Are batteries an environmental problem? Do electric cars work in cold weather? Are there enough charging points? And when does an electric car make financial sense?
Hop in and join us on a road trip in the name of science.

entry.title: Blue and green photoreceptor cells “see” differently

media:group.media:title: Blue and green photoreceptor cells “see” differently
media:group.media:description:
The human eye has four types of photoreceptor cells: rods for night vision and three types of cones for daylight vision – blue, green and red. All of them use the same molecule to detect light. But a tiny molecular difference causes them to respond to different colours of light. 👉 For more information: https://www.psi.ch/en/node/74372

media:group.media:title: 🧬💻 Cancer diagnosis using algorithms 💻🧬
media:group.media:description:
The prick of a needle, a few drops of blood – and a learning algorithm. Researchers at the PSI Paul Scherrer Institut are combining microscopy, cell biology, and artificial intelligence to detect subtle changes in the cell nucleus.
What makes this special: The AI recognises patterns in chromatin – compactly packed genetic material in the cell nucleus, which undergoes changes in cancer even before symptoms can be seen. This could open new avenues in the early detection of cancer and in monitoring therapeutic treatments. PSI researcher G.V. Shivashankar and his team show how research and computing power are working together – to enable the diagnostics of the future.

entry.title: No pumps, no power – how a reactor cools itself

media:group.media:title: No pumps, no power – how a reactor cools itself
media:group.media:description:
Researchers at the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI have tested passive cooling systems for small modular reactors at the globally unique PANDA facility. The principle: A pipe through which cool water circulates – driven solely by density differences. No electricity needed, no pumps.
The experiments provide spatially resolved measurement data under controlled conditions for the first time: 🌡️ The cooling system operates stably under various pressure conditions 📊 Around 1,450 sensors provide data for computer simulations 🔬 New insights into the role of air stratification in the containment vessel
The results are an important step towards the approval of future generations of reactors– and demonstrate that passive safety is not just theoretical.
📄 Learn more: https://www.psi.ch/en/news/media-releases/cooling-without-pumps-new-measurement-data-for-modular-reactors
